content.title: About
content.content: Sesame (Sesamum indicum) seeds are tiny oily seeds that come in white, golden, and black. They have a nutty, slightly sweet flavor that comes out especially after toasting. Sesame is sprinkled on buns, salads, and dishes, and is made into tahini, halva, oil, and the paste for hummus.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sesame is one of the oldest oilseed crops.
Sesame is made into tahini, halva, and sesame oil.
The phrase open sesame is linked to the way ripe sesame pods burst open and scatter their seeds.
Black sesame usually has its hull and contains more calcium, while white sesame is more often hulled.
Sesame is widely used in Asian, Middle Eastern, and Mediterranean cuisines.

items.title: Contains calcium and magnesium
items.content: These minerals are needed for bones, muscles, and nerves.

items.title: Contains iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals support oxygen transport and immunity.

items.title: Contains lignans
items.content: Sesamin and sesamolin are compounds with antioxidant properties.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: Most of the fat in sesame is mono- and polyunsaturated.

items.title: Source of protein and fiber
items.content: Sesame provides plant protein and fiber, especially when unhulled.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Sesame is recognized as a major food allergen, and allergy to it can be severe.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Sesame is high in calories, so portions should be small.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Sesame contains oxalates, which people prone to kidney stones may need to limit.

items.title: Whole seeds
items.content: Whole seeds may be poorly digested; it is better to chew them well or use them ground or as tahini.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: To bring out the flavor, lightly toast sesame in a dry pan until golden. Sprinkle it on buns, salads, vegetables, rice, and noodles, add it to dough, or make it into tahini, hummus, gomashio, and sauces. Small amounts are best.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store sesame in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For long-term storage, keep it in the refrigerator or freezer, because the oils can turn rancid. After opening, store tahini in a cool place or in the refrigerator. Discard seeds that smell rancid.
